newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: CALL TO LINK ZIMBABWE EXPORT ZONES TO NEIGHBOURS.
newsitem.headline: CALL TO LINK ZIMBABWE EXPORT ZONES TO NEIGHBOURS.

text.p: Zimbabwe should use its unfolding export processing zones (EPZs) to help drive general economic development in southern Africa, a leading local economic analyst said on Monday.

Mike Humphrey, managing director of Gemini Consulting, said at a seminar on EPZs that Zimbabwe could develop a Harare-Beira corridor, linking the Zimbabwe capital to Mozambique's Indian Ocean port city -- one of its main trade routes.

"The South African government has launched what it calls the Maputo Development Corridor. For Zimbabwe, most of the infrastructure is in place, or being provided in the immediate future, for an equivalent Beira Development Corridor," he said.

Humphrey, a former director for trade development at national trade promotion agency Zimtrade, pointed to several private sector projects on the outskirts of Harare, a proposed industrial park on the Beira route and a possible EPZ in Mutare, Zimbabwe's eastern border town, as schemes that would help underpin the corridor.

He urged President Robert Mugabe's government to consider his proposal to site EPZs on the Harare-Beira route, and to champion the construction of a four-track highway between the two cities -- an expansion of the existing two-lane road, railway and oil pipeline Beira (transport) Corridor.
The Harare-Beira Development Corridor may help boost Zimbabwe's currently sluggish manufacturing sector, he said.

"If my hypothesis that an emerging Harare-Beira growth axis is to become the future expansion for Zimbabwe's manufacturing sector is correct, then EPZs have a very important role in ensuring its success," he said.
"What I am looking at is development at a regional level, where our projects or EPZs will spur economic activity and development in neighbouring states," Humphrey said.

There was room, he said, for the private sector to lead this process by undertaking projects such as constructing, under a Build Own, Operate and Transfer (BOOT) scheme, solid highways linking Zimbabwe's major industrial centres with its regional export points.

Zimbabwe adopted an EPZ programme earlier this year, and so far only four projects have been licensed and five others are under consideration, well below the floods of applications Zimbabwean authorities initially expected.
